newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch trade plays down impact of soy protests.
newsitem.headline: Dutch trade plays down impact of soy protests.

text.p: Dutch trade sources played down any market impact from controversy over the import of new, genetically modified soybeans into Europe from the U.S. 1996 crop.
"I don't think its going to have a big effect, it will go away after a while," said Arie van Dijk of statisticians Stigevo on Wednesday.
"There may be a physchological effect on consumers."
Traders said old crop beans may be favoured over new crop, but that was only a short-term possibility.
On a day of protests around Europe by environmental group Greenpeace, Dutch traders said it was impossible to separate the new variety from normal ones.
"What can we do as traders," one said. "It's logistically impossible to keep these beans apart from others."
The beans, developed by U.S. company Monsanto, are resistant to the Roundup pesticide, also produced by Monsanto, and are being harvested for the first time this year from nearly one million acres.
"Whose to say a farmer in the States isn't going to mix up the two types of beans after harvest," another trader said.

One the main targets for the protests has been Anglo-Dutch food manufacturer Unilever, but a spokesman said the U.S. and European authorities had declared the beans safe and the company had reached the same conclusion.

The Dutch government, while sympathetic to consumer wishes on product information, has said it can do nothing to stop the soybeans entering the food chain. Instead it said it will launch a publicity campaign to tell consumers about them.
"You have to be open about this and tell the consumer that this type of soyabean is coming to Europe," Dutch farm minister Jozias van Aartsen told a news briefing last week.
"You can't tell where exactly these modified soybeans have been used. It vanishes into the whole (food) chain," he said.
